thesis.headline: The thinking behind it.
thesis.lead: Every Vibe plugin follows the same architectural playbook — an Apache-licensed spec that makes the claims checkable, not aspirational.
thesis.quote: A plugin should be more useful on its tenth run than on its first — not because the user learned it, but because it learned the user.
paragraphs: The Self-Evolving Plugin Framework is three disciplines stacked on top of each other: self-repair, self-teach, self-evolve. A plugin that can fix itself when it breaks, teach itself what the user actually wanted, and rewrite its own guidance when the pattern repeats. Each discipline earns its rung on a five-level maturity ladder — sixteen named patterns across the climb, one Apache-licensed spec, and a scorecard so the claims are checkable, not aspirational.

Vibe Cartographer sits at Level 3.5 right now — the highest rung any public plugin has reached — and every new plugin we ship gets benchmarked against the same ladder. The framework isn't marketing. It's how we keep the work honest when nobody's watching.

sections.heading: Deterministic engine, LLM only where it earns it.
paragraphs: The engine is deterministic and offline. It never calls an LLM or MCP — it reads local JSONL transcripts and a few cache files. The narrative read, the decisions overlay, and the per-session tags come from the /vibe-insights skill, where the LLM lives, and are handed to the engine as files. That keeps the analytics reproducible and the tool marketplace-portable.

Personal by default. Every ~/.claude* source on your machine is included and synced-eligible — no config to get started. Cross-machine works through tiny per-machine indexes you sync (Syncthing or anything that moves a folder); the report merges every machine. When you need to wall off an employer or client, mark a source or repo private — it stays in your own report but never leaves its origin box. Runs fully standalone; the optional cc-logs package keeps token numbers aligned with sibling tools like Sanduhr. Decisions are MCP-agnostic: a file, or your dashboard.
sections.callout: No telemetry. Everything stays on your machine — and anything you mark private never leaves the box it came from.

sections.heading: Three layers, one classifier, fixes you can ship.
paragraphs: vibe-sec separates security into three layers that compound. Hygiene is fully automatable: secrets out of source, headers added, CORS locked down. Architecture requires understanding how the app is built — does the auth actually protect the routes it claims to? Threat modeling asks what the realistic attack vectors are given this app's deployment context, and proposes a model for you to validate.

The classifier is what keeps it from being generic. The same finding — say, missing rate limiting — might be critical for a payment API and informational for a personal static site. vibe-sec classifies your app first (prototype → regulated enterprise); the tier sets the bar, not a one-size-fits-all checklist.

sections.heading: A tour you own, fully instrumented.
paragraphs: When the verdict is build, Phase 2 emits a drop-in TypeScript module: a spotlightSteps.ts config array and a spotlightTour.ts runner with start(onDone), SSR guard, progress indicator (“3 of 5”), and persistent replay export. Same ownership model as shadcn — you own the generated code from day one.

The anchor-injection pass adds data-tour="<kebab-semantic-name>" attributes via a jscodeshift codemod, auto-injecting only the provably safe subset and routing everything ambiguous to a REVIEW_NEEDED.md with per-item reason codes. Phase 2 halts until you resolve that list. Steps are capped at 5 (default 3–4). The shape of the completion cliff is consistent across sources and grounded in cognitive-load theory — stated honestly as a conservative guardrail below a single-vendor observed curve, not a proven constant. sections.heading: Nine commands across the prompt lifecycle.

cards.reach: Reach for it on every PR that touches a prompt.

cards.title: Confidence-routed fix diffs.
cards.desc: Routes high-confidence findings to ready-to-apply diffs and lower-confidence ones to annotated review files. Backs up every prompt before touching it and keeps rollback explicit.
cards.reach: Reach for it after audit surfaces issues you want to fix.

cards.desc: Reads your product and audit history, then proposes concrete AI feature candidates grounded in what your current prompt surface already handles well.

cards.desc: Pulls a digest of model releases, capability changes, and pricing shifts relevant to your current stack. No eval calls — read-only.
cards.reach: Reach for it when a model update lands and you want to know if anything breaks.

cards.title: L3 self-improvement.
cards.desc: Reads vibe-prompt's own session and friction logs, then proposes concrete edits to its own SKILLs and evaluation templates. Never auto-applies.
cards.reach: Reach for it when the audit keeps missing something you're catching manually.

cards.title: State-aware router.
cards.desc: Reads your project state — last scan age, open audit findings, baseline freshness — and recommends the right next command. Asks before launching anything.
cards.reach: Reach for it when you're not sure where in the loop you are.

sections.heading: Scan, audit, eval, grade, fix — in that order.
paragraphs: The loop runs left to right: scan inventories every prompt site read-only, audit applies the F1–F13 taxonomy statically, eval runs behavioral tests against your production model behind a cost gate, grade rolls everything into a composite score compared against a monotonic baseline, and remediate routes confident fixes to diffs with backup and explicit rollback. Each step is a standalone call — run the whole loop or drop in at any stage.

The F1–F13 taxonomy covers 13 structural smell classes across five scoring dimensions: schema tightness (are outputs constrained or freeform?), persona consistency (does the assistant's identity hold across turns?), instruction clarity (are directives specific enough to survive model updates?), token efficiency (is the prompt spending tokens on things that matter?), and injection resistance (is user input sanitized before it reaches the model?). F10–F12 are the injection-surface smells — when those trigger, vibe-prompt hands off directly to vibe-sec, which carries the injection findings through its own security posture loop. The two plugins compose, neither depends on the other.

The eval step uses a calibrated LLM-judge: a secondary model call that scores the primary output against a rubric derived from your audit findings. Calibration means the judge's pass threshold is tuned against known-good and known-bad examples from your own baseline, not a generic rubric — so the score means something specific to your app. Every eval run costs real tokens; the cost gate ensures you confirm spend before anything goes out.
sections.callout: Read-only by default. Real model calls only on :eval, behind an explicit cost gate. Nothing leaves your machine except the eval request you confirm.

install.note: Read-only by default; real vendor calls only on :eval behind a cost gate. Composes with vibe-sec for injection handoff.

sections.heading: Five commands across the localization retrofit.
sections.lead: From a read-only readiness scan to the guarded mutation loop, every step is a direct call. It mutates only with per-file backups — and every re-run is idempotent.

cards.title: Classify every user-facing string.
cards.desc: Reads the codebase and tags every user-facing string by kind — JSX text, placeholder, aria-label, title, alt, toast, locale-sensitive date — then emits a six-block readiness brief. Read-only; nothing is changed.

cards.title: Catch the i18n gotchas first.
cards.desc: Audits the stack for the traps that bite retrofits: firebase-admin in SSR, structural-vs-presentational Intl, the timeZone decision, RTL surfaces, dynamic-route guard globs. Names them before they corrupt a render.
cards.reach: Reach for it when the stack is non-trivial and you want the landmines mapped.

cards.title: Extract, wire, translate, guard.
cards.desc: The confidence-routed mutation loop: extracts strings to catalogs, wires the components, translates, and guards the result. Mutates only with per-file backups; re-runs are idempotent. Deep on next-intl + App Router.
cards.reach: Reach for it when the scan looks right and you're ready to move strings safely.

cards.title: Health-check the localization.
cards.desc: Catalog parity, the jsx-no-literals ratchet, and the guards that keep the localization honest as the app grows — so a new untranslated string shows up as a failed check, not a shipped bug.
cards.reach: Reach for it on every PR after the first localization pass lands.

cards.title: State-aware router.
cards.desc: Reads where you are — scanned, wired, translated, guarded — and recommends the right next command. Asks before launching anything.
cards.reach: Reach for it when you're not sure where in the retrofit you are.

sections.heading: Scan, audit, localize, guard — codemod-safe.
paragraphs: The loop runs left to right: scan classifies every user-facing string read-only and writes a six-block readiness brief, audit names the stack-specific gotchas that corrupt i18n retrofits, localize runs the confidence-routed extract → wire → translate → guard codemod, and vitals holds the line afterward with catalog-parity and jsx-no-literals guards. Every mutation writes a per-file backup first, and every re-run is idempotent — run it twice and nothing doubles.

It is deep on next-intl + App Router: cookie-driven locale, a catalog parity guard, a jsx-no-literals ratchet that tightens as you translate, and the ESM jest patch the stack needs. For everything else there is a real adapter seam that reports an honest not-yet-implemented rather than mishandling a stack it doesn't fully understand — a decline you can trust beats a silent corruption.

It earned that trust by dogfooding on Celestia3: localizing most of a live app — 720 strings across ~67 components — surfaced four of vibe-lingual's own codemod bugs, and the safety rails caught every one before it reached a green branch. Structural-green ≠ works is the throughline — the tests passing is necessary, not sufficient; the dogfood on a real app was the truth at every scale.
sections.callout: Mutates only with per-file backups and idempotent re-runs. Deep on next-intl + App Router; an honest not-yet-implemented for the rest, never a silent mishandle.

sections.heading: Map, gate, prove. Refuse where it matters.
paragraphs: The access work runs in three stages: agent affordances → agent-facing API → MCP server. vibe-access owns the middle. It maps what your app already exposes, scaffolds what is missing, and writes it into a manifest an agent can read cold. The manifest is the embryo of your eventual MCP server, not the server itself; graduating it stays a deliberate, manual step.

Affordances are dev (env-gated, never ships) or prod-safe (runs under the caller's own auth, no elevated access). seed, reset, and capture can never be tagged prod-safe, and that is a refusal enforced at three layers: the manifest schema rejects it, the engine throws if you route around it, and the scaffolder will not apply a dev-tier file missing the vibe-access:dev-gate marker. There is no flag that lets a seed endpoint into production.

It is deep on Firebase Cloud Functions: hosting-rewrite route detection and ID-token auth mapping. Since v0.3.0 it also maps Streamlit apps, where every sidebar mode and page lands as a named finding and the scaffold is a dev-gated FastAPI sidecar bound to localhost. Next.js and Express report not-yet-implemented instead of guessing, and the agnostic path writes what you learned to an adapter-notes file that seeds the next real adapter. Dogfooded on WeSeeYouAtTheMovies: 84 routes scanned, 85 affordances, verify 76/85 with all 9 fails classified, and 7 plugin bugs surfaced and fixed in the same session with regression tests.
sections.callout: Seed, reset, and capture can never be prod-safe. A refusal, not a warning, enforced in the schema, the engine, and the scaffolder.

install.note: Scan and map are read-only against your source. Scaffold is backup-wrapped and dev-gated; verify is local-only unless you force it. Adapters for Firebase Cloud Functions and Streamlit; honest not-yet-implemented for other stacks.

vibe-glow.name: vibe-glow
vibe-glow.metaTitle: vibe-glow · Take an app from working to wanted. · 626Labs
vibe-glow.ogTitle: vibe-glow · Take an app from working to wanted.
vibe-glow.metaDescription: Claude Code plugin for UI and QOL beautification campaigns. Invents a design language, audits with Opus review lenses and a skeptic pass, ships fix batches re-reviewed until clean, then reveals the flagship. WinUI and web adapters. MIT. By 626Labs.
vibe-glow.h1: Take an app from working to wanted.
vibe-glow.subhead: vibe-glow runs a repeatable, gated beautification campaign: a measuring stick first, a skeptic-verified findings register next, then fix batches re-reviewed until clean, then the flagship release. Go app-wide with an invented design language, or scoped to one area with a goal in your own words. Consent is per stage, so one yes runs one stage.

terminal.label: vibe-glow ~
lines: [vibe-glow] No campaign state here. Full glow-up, or a focused fix?
→ you: focused, the settings screen should feel calmer
[vibe-glow] stage: identity · scope: settings screen
→ read-only — nothing captured, nothing written

sections.heading: Six commands, one campaign.
sections.lead: Start with the concierge and it runs the next right stage after you say yes. Or call any stage directly. Nothing auto-advances.

cards.title: Start here.
cards.desc: The concierge and the bare entry point. Asks whether you want a full glow-up or a focused fix, gathers what it needs, and runs each stage only after an explicit yes. You never need to know a stage name.
cards.reach: Reach for it when you want the whole campaign without learning the stages.

cards.title: Build the measuring stick.
cards.desc: Stage 0. Invents a design language for an app-wide campaign, or extracts a conventions brief for a scoped one. Captures the app's invariants, such as user theming, so reviewers know what they can't touch.
cards.reach: Reach for it before anyone judges a screen as good or bad.

cards.title: Find what's actually wrong.
cards.desc: Stage 1. Five Opus review lenses produce a findings register, and a skeptic pass faces every finding before it becomes work. Scoped campaigns audit only their scope, weighted toward your goal.
cards.reach: Reach for it when you want a ranked list you can defend, not a vibe.

cards.title: Ship one fix batch.
cards.desc: Stage 2, one wave per call. Branch, fix, review, re-capture, re-review until the surfaces measure clean. Every tally is re-derived from the register's rows, never carried forward from the last wave.
cards.reach: Reach for it when the register is approved and it's time to change pixels.

cards.title: Close the campaign.
cards.desc: Stage 3. The flagship release for an app-wide run, or a goal-check close-out for a scoped one. It re-derives the severity-4+ status from the register before it opens.
cards.reach: Reach for it when every high-severity finding is clean or explicitly waived.

cards.title: Where is the campaign.
cards.desc: Read-only. Stage, scope, adapter, invariants, findings tallies read from the register this invocation, and the wave ledger. No captures, no writes, no agents.
cards.reach: Reach for it when you're coming back to a campaign cold.

sections.heading: Measure first, skeptic second, ship third.
paragraphs: The campaign runs identity → audit → wave → reveal. Identity produces the measuring stick. Audit runs five Opus review lenses, and a skeptic pass tries to refute each finding before it becomes work. Waves ship fix batches and re-review until the surface measures clean. Reveal closes it out. Consent is per stage: one yes runs one stage.

Per-app invariants outrank findings. If the app has user theming, color belongs to the user and identity lives in structure. Scoreboard claims re-derive from register rows every time they're written; the commands record that a carried-forward scoreboard once cost a campaign an extra wave. Evidence like screenshots stays out of git, while state, measuring sticks, and the findings register are committed.

Evidence comes from two adapters: winui-powershell (window capture, UIA route maps, UIA tree dumps, and pixel sampling) and web-playwright. The first dogfood target was 626 Mod Launcher. Loggers and an evolve pass are deliberately deferred until they're earned.
sections.callout: One yes runs one stage. Nothing auto-advances, and every finding faces a skeptic before it becomes work.

install.note: Campaign state lives in .vibe-glow/state.json at your repo root. Evidence adapters cover WinUI (PowerShell capture) and web (Playwright).

vibe-runbook.name: vibe-runbook
vibe-runbook.metaTitle: vibe-runbook · A runbook that checks itself against the running system. · 626Labs
vibe-runbook.ogTitle: vibe-runbook · A runbook that checks itself against the running system.
vibe-runbook.metaDescription: Claude Code plugin for runbooks. Drafts one from what your repo can prove, classifies every claim, then walks the machine-checkable ones against an environment you name. Read-only, never spends, honest about what it could not check. MIT. By 626Labs.
vibe-runbook.h1: A runbook that checks itself against the running system.
vibe-runbook.subhead: A runbook says do X and you will see W. Nothing checks whether that is still true. vibe-runbook writes one by inspecting your app, then walks its claims against a running system — read-only, never spends, and honest about what it could not check. Every report says checked N of M enumerated.

terminal.label: vibe-runbook ~
lines: → pins, status assertions, receipts, questions · confidence reported
→ PASS · FAIL · BLOCKED · SPENDS · HUMAN · QUESTION
→ receipts reported, never failed · nothing written, nothing spent
→ checked N of M enumerated

sections.heading: Seven commands, from drafting a runbook to keeping it true.
sections.lead: Scan reads, walk checks, remediate rewrites, author drafts. The walk is read-only and never spends; the rewrite diffs by default and backs up every file it touches.

cards.title: Inventory every claim.
cards.desc: Reads a runbook and classifies each claim by shape: a pin, a status assertion, a past-tense receipt, a question. Ambiguity escalates to a question instead of a guess, and the extraction reports its own confidence.
cards.reach: Reach for it before you trust a runbook, to see what in it a machine can actually check.

cards.title: Check it against a named environment.
cards.desc: Walks the machine-checkable claims with six verdicts: PASS, FAIL, BLOCKED, SPENDS, HUMAN, QUESTION. Read-only, never spends, and --env is required. A missing credential hard-stops as BLOCKED with the exact ask instead of quietly walking your local machine.
cards.reach: Reach for it when you want to know which lines of the runbook are still true today.

cards.title: Fix the stale pin.
cards.desc: Rewrites a stale pin as the command that answers it where the reader has a shell, or as the list it was summarizing where they do not. Diffs by default; --apply writes, with a backup beside every file it touches.
cards.reach: Reach for it after a walk shows a pin that went stale.

cards.title: Draft the runbook from the repo.
cards.desc: Inspects the app and writes an operations runbook from what it can derive: a revision pin that answers itself, the run commands, deploy and rollback scripts where they exist, the names of the configuration keys. What a repo cannot tell you comes out as explicit questions. It proposes beside your runbook and never overwrites it.
cards.reach: Reach for it when the runbook does not exist yet, or the one you have was written from memory.

cards.title: Health of the local state.
cards.desc: Checks the local vibe-runbook state.
cards.reach: Reach for it when a run behaves oddly and you want to rule out the plugin's own state.

cards.title: Improve the plugin itself.
cards.desc: Reflects on past runs and proposes improvements to the plugin. Writes proposals; never edits a skill. Session logging is not wired yet, so it has little to draw from today.
cards.reach: Reach for it once the plugin has real runs behind it.

cards.title: State-aware router.
cards.desc: Reads what exists (a cached scan, a config, a runbook) and recommends one next move. Never walks or writes on its own.
cards.reach: Reach for it when you are not sure which step comes next.

sections.heading: Honest about what it could not check.
paragraphs: A document that says it tested 17 rooms is not lying when there are now 12. So a receipt is reported and never failed: past-tense coverage records drift because the world moved. Pins are different. A pin is a value that identifies the running system, and the walk checks it. Enumeration is mechanical and exhaustive, never sampled, and every report states checked N of M enumerated.

Four invariants hold on every walk. Credential preflight hard-stops. Nothing spends: a billable check is reported as SPENDS with what a full walk would cost, and never run. No secret is printed: shapes, statuses and counts only. The contract source beats the guess: when the runbook is ambiguous about an interface, it reads the route table or client definition.

It earned those on a real service. Walked read-only against a live Cloud Run service's hand-written smoke list, it returned 5 claims PASS, 3 FAIL, and 8 of 8 numbered steps unreachable. The write-guard probe sent a request that fails validation against a resource that does not exist, and found six routes answering 422 with the missing field name instead of 401. All six were fixed the same day and re-walked.

The author is just as plain about its limits. Run against two real applications that already carry hand-written runbooks, it fabricated nothing: it wrote only what it could verify, asked for the rest by name, and listed what it failed to gather. Expect questions, not a finished document. Most of a real operations runbook is not in the repository.
sections.callout: Read-only, never spends, never prints a secret. No telemetry, and no outbound calls beyond the walk you named.

install.note: Read-only walk, and --env is required. Remediate diffs by default and backs up before --apply writes. Node engine with no runtime dependencies.

vibe-recall.name: vibe-recall
vibe-recall.metaTitle: vibe-recall · Have you already built this? Check your own repos first. · 626Labs
vibe-recall.ogTitle: vibe-recall · Have you already built this? Check your own repos first.
vibe-recall.metaDescription: Claude Code plugin that surfaces prior art from your own repos while you spec the next one. Indexes your estate into shallow cards, ranks them against a phrase or spec file, and verifies the hit at current HEAD before it claims anything. MIT. By 626Labs.
vibe-recall.h1: Have you already built this? Check your own repos first.
vibe-recall.subhead: vibe-recall indexes the repos you've already written and answers one question while you spec the next feature: have I built something like this? It ranks shallow cards against your phrase or spec file, then re-reads the winning hit live at its current HEAD before it says anything about the source. A stale card can point. Only a live read can claim.

terminal.label: vibe-recall ~
lines: [vibe-recall] Checking this repo's own source first... done
→ ranking indexed cards · code fields outrank prose
→ each hit carries a why line: which fields and terms fired
[vibe-recall] Re-reading the hit at current HEAD...
→ cited paths opened live · card treated as a lead, not a citation
→ handoff: vibe-taker moves the code, you run it

sections.heading: Six commands, from index to verified brief.
sections.lead: Index the estate, sweep it for prior art, then verify one hit live. It never writes code and never edits anything inside a repo it indexes.

cards.title: Map the estate.
cards.desc: Walks your configured estate root and builds or refreshes a shallow card per in-scope repo. Duplicate clones collapse to one canonical card, and diverged pairs get named for you to resolve instead of picked silently.
cards.reach: Reach for it on first run, and whenever your repos have moved since the last index.

cards.title: Rank prior art against a phrase or spec.
cards.desc: Takes a phrase or a spec file path, checks the current repo's own source first, then ranks indexed cards. Scoring is deterministic and explains itself. Forks and vendored checkouts are excluded by default, and zero hits comes back as a real answer.
cards.reach: Reach for it before you write the spec for something that feels familiar.

cards.title: Verify one hit at current HEAD.
cards.desc: Re-reads the named repo live and writes up what is actually there. It is the only skill allowed to author a claim about source. Ends with a handoff to vibe-taker, which does the moving.
cards.reach: Reach for it when a sweep hit looks real and you're about to lean on it.

cards.title: Promote a card from shallow to deep.
cards.desc: Reads a repo's actual source and records its real features on the card. With no argument it takes the top of the demand-ranked queue: non-deep cards ordered by recall hits, then last-commit recency.
cards.reach: Reach for it when the same repo keeps surfacing and its card is still thin.

cards.title: Check index coverage and hygiene.
cards.desc: Reports repos indexed, deep cards, queue depth, diverged pairs, foreign repos by name, scan-truncated counts, and secret-file skips. Also flags a missing runtime dependency with the fix.
cards.reach: Reach for it when a sweep feels thin and you want to know why.

cards.title: State-aware router.
cards.desc: Reads your config and index state and recommends one next command. It never fires index or anything mutating on its own.
cards.reach: Reach for it when you're not sure what to run next.

sections.heading: The index suggests. Only a live read claims.
paragraphs: A card holds shapes, never content: symbol names, dependency names, entrypoint paths, and short claim strings pulled from README and CLAUDE.md. No file bodies. Files that are .env-shaped by name, or that trip a secret-shape scan by content, are skipped. The index is a map of your estate, not a mirror of it.

Because a card is a snapshot from whenever index last ran, it is good enough to rank and point, never good enough to quote. /vibe-recall:brief opens the file again in the current session, at the repo's current HEAD, before it writes a word about the source. The fork filter reads authorship from git history and fails open: a repo it can't classify is never treated as foreign.

Walls are refusals. You set tenant walls in first-run setup, nothing ships pre-seeded, and a path under a wall is never indexed, ranked, or named in the index. There is no override flag. A UserPromptSubmit hook can surface a banner when your prompt reads like you're about to build something. Cards and config live in the plugin's local data home, never inside an indexed repo, and there is no cross-machine sync.
sections.callout: Cards store shapes, never file bodies. Walls have no override flag. Zero hits is a real answer.

install.note: First use runs setup: estate root, tenant walls, optional GitHub accounts for remote-only listing. Needs Node; one runtime dependency (ajv) installs with the plugin, and vitals tells you if it didn't. Indexes only your own estate root, no public code search.
